lesson.title: One Line, Many Variables: Multiple Assignment
lesson.summary: Python allows several variables to be assigned in a single statement, either by unpacking a sequence of values into matching variable names or by chaining equal signs to give several variables the same value at once.
lesson.body:
Ordinary Variable Assignment gives one variable a value with a single = sign, but Python supports two shortcuts for handling several variables together. The first is unpacking: x, y, z = 1, 2, 3 assigns 1 to x, 2 to y, and 3 to z, all in one statement. Python evaluates the right-hand side first, building the group of values (1, 2, 3), and then matches them up position by position with the names on the left. The number of values on each side must match exactly, or Python raises a ValueError rather than guessing which value belongs where.

The second shortcut is chained assignment, where the same value is given to multiple variables at once: total = count = 0 sets both total and count to 0 in a single line. This is handy for initializing several counters or accumulators before a loop begins, since it avoids writing total = 0 and count = 0 as two separate statements that say almost the same thing.

The most elegant use of unpacking is swapping two variables without any extra temporary variable. Given a = 5 and b = 10, the statement a, b = b, a swaps their values. Trace it carefully: Python first builds the right-hand pair using the current values, (10, 5), before touching either variable, and only then assigns the first element to a and the second to b. So a becomes 10 and b becomes 5, a clean swap in one line. Many other languages require a third, temporary variable to hold one value while the swap happens; Python's unpacking makes that unnecessary because the entire right-hand side is evaluated before any assignment occurs.

It helps to see multiple assignment as a convenience layered directly on top of the single-variable assignment already familiar from Variable Assignment, rather than a completely new idea. Every multiple assignment statement could, in principle, be rewritten as several separate assignment statements; the shortcut exists purely to reduce repetition and to visually group variables that are conceptually related, such as coordinates x, y = 3, 7 or the three parts of a date year, month, day = 2026, 8, 29.

It is worth being precise about what chained assignment actually does under the hood, since it looks like one statement but behaves like several. In total = count = 0, Python evaluates the single value 0 exactly once, and then binds both names, total and count, to that same value in sequence. For an immutable value like the integer 0, this distinction rarely matters in practice, since neither variable can change the underlying value the other one points to; later reassigning total on its own, such as total += 5, only affects total and leaves count untouched at 0.

Used well, multiple assignment makes initialization code shorter and easier to scan, since a reader can see at a glance that several variables are being set up together rather than scrolling through a long list of near-identical single-variable lines. Unpacking in particular is worth reaching for whenever a group of values naturally belongs together, since x, y = 3, 7 communicates that x and y form a coordinate pair far more clearly than two separate lines would.
